newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK rates to stay put, Reuters poll shows.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK rates to stay put, Reuters poll shows.

text.p: A shock rise in British interest rates, which caught financial markets by surprise, is likely to be the last beforee an election, a Reuters survey showed.

Fifteen out of 20 analysts contacted after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke upped base rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent agreed that rates will go no higher before an election which must be held before next May.

"There is enough reason to doubt from an economic perspective whether further tightening is required. The political imperative in any case will prevent them rising," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston.
But a sizeable minority -- five of the 20 polled -- said they would expect another rise before the election.
Contributors were asked where the peak of the interest rate cycle would be and nine of the 20 said they expected base rates to rise as high as seven percent.
Forecasts for the peak ranged between 6.25 and 8.50 percent.

By the end of 1997, no matter which party wins the election, base rates may have to rise by three quarters of a point to 6.75 percent, the survey showed. Predictions for end-1997 ranged from 6.25 percent to 8.50 percent.
Sharda Persaud, European economist at San Paulo Bank, believes that the recent sharp fall in unemployment, and growing consumer confidence made higher base rates in 1997 inevitable.

"They (interest rates) will also be heading upwards in the U.S.," Persaud said. In September the British jobless total fell by 35,600 and the unemployment rate fell to 7.4 percent from 7.5 percent in August. Analysts point to this, and also average earnings figures, as sources of price pressure.
Underlying average earnings were revised to four percent from the initial estimate of 3.75 percent in July and stuck at that level in August.
"The markets may react to the UK rate rise as a sign that the interest rate cycle has turned for the world," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais.
Market speculation that the Federal Reserve would make a pre-emptive strike on inflation has in recent months died out.
But many analysts believe that after the presidential election on November 5, a higher Federal Funds target rate from 5.25 percent will be on the agenda.
The lowest forecast for British base rate at the end of next year was made by DKB International at 6.25 percent. Their forecast for the peak of the cycle was also 6.25 percent.
"I don't think they will go much higher, the structural changes in the UK have created a disinflationary environment," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
"Attempts by retailers to push up prices are just not sticking and consumers are price conscious," he said.
